en: The Scripture on the Eight Teachers Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the layman Zhi Qian of the Yuezhi country during the Wu dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. At that time...
There was a brahmin named Yajña who came to where the Buddha was.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"A heterodox brahmin is now standing outside, wishing to consult you regarding his doubts."
The World-Honored One said,
"Bring him forward.
The brahmin then stepped forward and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
The Celestial Honored One said,
"Take your seat. The brahmin took his seat, and after a short while, he withdrew and sat back down, saying:

"I have heard that the Way of the Buddha is vast and profound in its meaning, expansive and boundless; there is nothing it does not bring to fulfillment, and no living being it does not deliver. Majestic and sublime, it is like the moon among the stars; its divine wisdom is wondrously penetrating, making it the King among all sages—something the various devas cannot attain and something the common people have never heard."
"I pray that you will open my blindness and darkness, and dispel my ignorance.
Whom did you serve as a teacher to attain such supreme honor?
The World-Honored One sighed and said:
"How excellent is this question!
It opens up the great practice.
My teachers in previous lives are too numerous to enumerate; "
I have now spontaneously attained the divine radiance of the Way; I have no teacher.
Nevertheless, there are eight teachers from whom I have acquired this through the experience of punishment and execution;
some were executed by royal law, their destruction extending even to their clans and lineages.
Upon death, they enter hell, where they are scorched, boiled, flogged, and lashed, enduring every kind of torment; though they seek death, they cannot find it.

Only when their retribution is exhausted do they emerge, perhaps as hungry ghosts or as animals, where they are slaughtered, dismembered, flayed, and torn apart; at each death, the blade is renewed, and as their spirits transmigrate, they continue to prey upon one another.
"I have seen that the retribution for one who kills is such as this; I dare not kill again.
This is my first teacher.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The killer's mind is unbenevolent, causing the strong and the weak to injure and maim one another.
Killing living beings brings retribution upon birth; it accumulates enmity through kalpas.
One suffers the crime of a short life and dies, encountering violent calamities in terror."
"Because I fear this, I have subdued the palace of Māra with a mind of loving-kindness.
The Buddha said:
"The second refers to theft and robbery, forcibly seizing the wealth of others."
Or they may be subjected to punishments of wealth, blades, and staves by their masters, whereby they are instantly disintegrated;

or they may be arrested and imprisoned by the king’s law, undergoing flogging, caning, and the simultaneous infliction of the five poisons, being executed in the marketplace until their entire clan is reduced to ashes.
Upon death, they enter hell, where they must cup their hands to hold fire and pour molten copper into their mouths; though they seek death, they cannot find it.

When their retribution is exhausted, they emerge only to become hungry ghosts (*preta*); when they wish to drink water, the water turns into pus, and whatever food they desire turns into charcoal. Their bodies are constantly burdened with heavy loads, and manifold afflictions follow them.
"Or one may become an animal, dying only to have one's flesh cut again and provided to others to repay debts from past lives.
I have seen that the retribution for a thief is such as this; therefore, I dare not steal again."
"These are my two teachers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The thief takes what is not given, plundering and stealing the wealth and treasures of others."
Regardless of how many die, those who harbor anger and grief receive the bodies of six domestic animals upon death to repay their past debts;
it is because I fear this that I have abandoned my home to practice the Way.
The Buddha said:
"The third is sexual misconduct, which means violating another's wife.
Whether it is discovered by her husband or relatives, one will incur calamity at that time, suffering punishment such as being struck with blades or staves."
Or they may be arrested by the royal law and cast into prison, where they are subjected to cruel and poisonous torture, and executed in the marketplace.
Upon death, they enter hell and are laid upon iron beds;
or they embrace copper pillars while the hell-demons kindle fires to burn their bodies.
When their retribution in hell is exhausted, they shall further become animals.

If they are reborn as humans, their households will be licentious and disorderly; they will violate the Buddha’s distant Dharma, not associate with the virtuous, and constantly harbor fear, experiencing much peril and little peace.
"Because I see this, I do not dare to commit sexual misconduct.
This is my third teacher.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
“Lust is an impure practice; through delusion, one loses the right path.
The spirit, soul, and vital breaths scatter; life is harmed and one dies prematurely.
One undergoes the punishment of stubborn ignorance and wastefulness, and after death, falls again into the evil realms.”
"Because I fear these things, I have abandoned my home to delight in the forests and marshes.
The Buddha said:
"The four are: harsh speech, double-tongued speech, false speech, and frivolous speech."
Those who slander others without cause, or defame the Triple Gem, shall have their tongues subjected to flogging and even the destruction of their entire families.
After death, they enter hell, where the spirits and deities within pull out their tongues and plow them with oxen;
molten copper is poured into their mouths, yet they find no way to die.
When their retribution is exhausted, they emerge from that state only to become animals, constantly eating grass and thorns.

If they later become human beings, their words will not be believed; their mouths will perpetually stink, and they will frequently encounter slander and abusive speech. They will have nightmares whenever they lie down, and though they possess mouths, they will be unable to savor the supreme flavor of the Buddha’s sutras.
"Because I see this, I do not dare to engage in harsh speech.
These are my four teachers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The deceiver has four faults: slander and flattery harm the virtuous;
they receive the retribution of being dull, deaf, and blind; they are stammering and foul-mouthed;
and in their madness they cannot speak, and upon death they enter the prison of the uprooted tongue."
"I have cultivated the four purities of speech, thereby attaining for myself the eight qualities of voice.
The Buddha said:
"The fifth refers to the indulgence in alcohol."

Alcohol is a toxic vapor that primarily brings about all manner of evils: it destroys the royal way and extinguishes benevolent grace; it causes ministers to be arrogant toward their superiors and loyalty and respect to decay; it leads fathers to lose propriety and mothers to lose compassion; it makes sons violent and rebellious and the path of filial piety fail; it causes husbands to break their promises and wives to become extravagant and licentious; it incites strife among the nine branches of the clan and squanders wealth and property. There is no ruin of a state or peril to one’s person that does not stem from this.
The ways in which wine disrupts the Dao number thirty-six.
Having seen these things, I have renounced wine and do not drink it;
this is my fifth teacher.
The Buddha then spoke in verse:
"The intoxicated commit filial impiety; resentment and calamity arise from within.
They delude the pure and noble, and they disorder virtue and ruin the chaste."

"Therefore, I do not drink wine; with a compassionate heart I save all living beings, and through pure wisdom I transcend the eight difficulties, thereby personally attaining the realization of the Way.
Thus spoke the Buddha.

"Sixth is old age. Now, the suffering of old age consists of white hair, falling teeth, blurred vision, and dull hearing; vigor departs and decay arrives; the skin slackens and the face wrinkles; the hundred joints ache, walking becomes extreme hardship, and one groans when sitting down or rising up; filled with sorrow, grief, vexation, and pain;
consciousness and spirit gradually fade away, and one immediately forgets what has just occurred."
Life is fleeting and its end draws near; speaking of this, my words flow with tears.
Having witnessed impermanence and calamities such as these, I have set out to seek the Way, desiring no longer to be subject to them.
"These were my six teachers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I contemplate that the world is impermanent; Human life must inevitably reach old age."
In youth one flourishes, but with the passing of days one declines and grows frail; the body withers and the hair turns white.
Through anxiety and toil, a hundred ailments arise, and one suffers from grief and pain while sitting or rising.
It is because I fear this that I have abandoned my home to practice the Way.
The Buddha said:
"The seventh refers to illness and emaciation.
When the flesh has wasted away until the bones stand out and all the joints ache, it is as if one were being flogged with a staff."
The four elements advance and retreat, rendering the hands and feet useless;
vital energy is utterly exhausted, requiring assistance for both sitting and lying down;
the mouth becomes parched and the lips wither, while the tendons snap and the nose cracks.
The eyes do not see forms, nor do the ears hear sounds;
impurities flow forth, and the body lies upon them;
the mind harbors suffering and affliction, and every word uttered is one of sorrow.

Now I observe that the people of this world, though in the prime of their years and endowed with vigorous strength, and though their radiant complexions are brilliant, find their blessings exhausted and misfortune arrive; impermanence brings a hundred transformations.
Seeing these afflictions, I have therefore set out to seek the Way, not wishing to undergo them again.
"These were my seven teachers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"When one reflects on the time of aging and decline, A hundred ailments arise all at once."
When the water dries up, the fire is extinguished; the knife and wind dissolve the body’s form.
The bones separate and the sinews and veins snap; the great life must inevitably fall.
It is for fear of this that I seek the Way, vowing not to be born again.
The Buddha said:
"The eighth refers to human death.
The four hundred and four diseases arise simultaneously; "
When the four great elements disperse, the soul and spirit find no rest;
the wind departs and the breath ceases, the fire is extinguished and the body grows cold—the wind first, followed by the fire, and then the soul departs;
the body remains rigid, with nothing further to be known.
Within ten days, the flesh rotted and blood flowed; it became bloated, putrid, and foul-smelling, such that not a single part was fit to take.
Worms within the body began to eat its own flesh;

the sinews and veins completely decayed, and the joints of the bones fell apart. The skull lay in one place, while the spine, ribs, shoulders, arms, thighs, shins, feet, and toes each lay in separate locations.
Flying birds and running beasts vied with one another to come and devour it;
gods, dragons, ghosts, spirits, emperors, kings, commoners, the wealthy and the poor, the noble and the lowly—none were exempt from this affliction.
"Seeing this transformation, I therefore went forth to seek the Way, not wishing to change it.
These are my eight teachers.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"I contemplate only old age, sickness, and death, the great afflictions of the three realms.
When merit is exhausted and life comes to an end, the breath ceases in the Yellow Springs;
the body decays and returns to dust, while the soul follows according to causes and conditions."
"It is because I fear this that I study the Way and ascend to Nirvāṇa.

Upon hearing what the Buddha had said, the brahmin’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he immediately attained the fruit of the Path (srotāpatti), received the five precepts, and became a lay follower (*upāsaka*)—one who does not kill, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not deceive, observes filial piety, and does not drink intoxicants—and he departed with joy.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Eight Teachers of Humanity.
